analysis.one_liner: Bans grocery stores from setting individualized prices using customer surveillance data.
analysis.headline: The consumer-protection bill has sat in two House committees with zero cosponsors and no vote since it was introduced in April 2026.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it illegal to use algorithms fed by surveillance data — things like shopping history, location, biometrics, or purchased personal data — to set a customized price for food or groceries for a specific shopper. It keeps ordinary practices like senior discounts and opt-in loyalty rewards legal, so long as the rules are disclosed and the data is used only to administer the discount. The Federal Trade Commission, state attorneys general, and individual shoppers could all enforce the ban, and shoppers could not be forced into arbitration for these claims.
analysis.who_benefits: Grocery shoppers. Today, a store using electronic shelf labels, loyalty apps, facial recognition, or purchased data could quietly charge one person more than another for the same item based on what it knows about them. The bill bans that practice outright, while keeping across-the-board discounts, cost-based price differences, and opt-in loyalty rewards legal. Shoppers who are charged anyway gain enforcement tools: a private right of action with at least $3,000 per violation, triple damages for willful violations, attorney's fees, and the right to sue in court rather than forced arbitration. State attorneys general can also sue on residents' behalf.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Grocery shoppers and their personal data

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits 'surveillance-based price setting' — using an automated decision system fed by surveillance data (personal information, genetic information, behavior, biometrics, or data gathered or purchased from third parties) to set a customized price for a specific person or group for food, groceries, or agricultural commodities.

Protects ordinary discounts while banning individualized pricing: differences based only on real costs, discounts for broad groups like teachers, veterans, seniors, and students, and opt-in loyalty or rewards program discounts stay legal — but only if eligibility is clearly disclosed, offered uniformly, and the data is used solely to administer the discount, not for profiling, targeted ads, or individualized prices.

Gives shoppers and enforcers real teeth: the FTC can treat violations as unfair or deceptive practices; state attorneys general can sue for the greater of actual damages or $3,000 per violation; individuals can sue for the same amount, with triple damages for willful violations, attorney's fees, a 5-year window to sue, and invalidation of pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for these claims.

analysis.who_pays: Grocery chains, online food sellers, and any company that sells or uses consumer data for pricing would bear the cost. They would have to publish procedures 180 days before using covered discounts, prove their data is accurate, let consumers correct it, and face FTC action, state suits, and private lawsuits with statutory damages of $3,000 per violation. Data brokers and pricing-software vendors would lose a market: their data and tools could no longer be used to individualize grocery prices. Retailers would also lose the ability to charge their most price-insensitive customers more.
analysis.who_pays_short: Grocery chains, data brokers, pricing-software vendors

drawbacks.text: The bill does not directly lower any grocery price. It bans a personalized-pricing practice, but the text contains no finding that it is already widespread, and grocery prices are driven by many other factors it does not touch — so its title promises more than its mechanism delivers.

It entrenches loyalty programs as the legal channel for shopper data: a store can still enroll customers in a rewards program and use that surveillance data, as long as it is used 'solely' to administer discounts — a line that may be hard to police in practice.

The $3,000-per-violation statutory damages plus mandatory attorney's fees create a litigation exposure that does not require showing a shopper was actually overcharged, which could invite abusive suits against retailers.

A blanket ban also rules out the upside of personalized pricing: in principle, algorithms can identify shoppers on tight budgets and offer them lower prices. The bill's loyalty-program exception preserves some of this, but any discount outside the defined exceptions becomes illegal.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For shoppers, the upside is protection against a practice — algorithmic personalized pricing on essentials like food — where the harm is invisible at the register: you never know you were charged more than the person next to you. The costs fall mostly on retailers and data companies, though honest supporters should admit the bill's headline overpromises: it does not lower today's grocery prices, and its loyalty-program carve-out leaves a large data-collection channel open. The statutory damages could also produce opportunistic litigation. On balance it is a genuine, if narrow, consumer protection with real enforcement power.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in April 2026 and sent to two House committees, and nothing has happened since — no cosponsors, no committee vote, no floor action.

narrative.text: Rep. Chris Pappas introduced the bill on April 9, 2026, with no cosponsors.
The Speaker referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, the Judiciary Committee, splitting jurisdiction between them.
As of the latest action record, neither committee has taken it up; the cosponsor list stands at zero.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has won or lost on the merits: grocery retailers, data brokers, and pricing-software vendors remain free to use algorithmic and surveillance-based pricing exactly as before, because the bill has not moved an inch.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Grocery and data companies, so far

for.name: Chris Pappas
for.role: U.S. Representative, New Hampshire (introduced the bill)
for.what_they_did: Introduced H.R. 8229, the Lower Grocery Prices Act, on April 9, 2026.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred and no member besides the sponsor has taken a position: the bill's only sponsor is a Democrat and its cosponsor list is zero, so no partisan pattern is visible yet.

industries.industry: Grocery retailers and big-box food sellers
industries.note: The bill bans the core of emerging 'surveillance pricing': using loyalty data, shelf-label systems, biometrics, or purchased data to charge individual shoppers different prices for the same food. Stores could no longer quietly charge their least price-sensitive customers more.
Surveillance data 'gathered, purchased, or otherwise acquired' could no longer feed individualized grocery prices, cutting off a would-be market for selling personal data into retail pricing.

The bill explicitly legalizes discounts through opt-in loyalty, membership, and rewards programs, so stores' existing data-collection channel survives — but only if data is used solely to administer the discount, not for profiling or individualized prices.

Automated decision systems, including machine-learning tools, could not be used to set individualized food prices from surveillance data, shrinking a market these vendors are building for grocery clients.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and jurisdiction split across two committees, the bill follows the most common path in Congress: it is likely to sit in Energy and Commerce and Judiciary without a hearing, markup, or floor vote, and die when this Congress ends on January 3, 2027, unless the sponsor attracts cosponsors or pushes for a hearing in the months remaining.
